title: Row, then column
prompt:
In module 5, `sbp[2]` picked the second value of a vector. A data frame
has two directions, so its square brackets take two things, separated by a
comma: **the row first, then the column.**

```r
patients[4, "age"]
```

Click the value this picks out.
hint: Count down four rows, then find the `age` column.

response.other:
Row first, then column: the number before the comma is the row, and the
name after it is the column. Count down to row 4, then across to `age`.

options.feedback:
Right — 48. Row 4, column `age`. The comma is doing all the work: what
comes before it chooses rows, what comes after it chooses columns.
That one rule is behind almost every bracket you'll see in a data
frame.

title: Leaving a side blank
prompt:
Nothing is written after the comma this time. What does this give you?

```r
patients[2, ]
```
hint: A blank doesn't mean "nothing". Which side of the comma is the 2 on?
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: All of row 2 — that patient's age, blood type, blood pressure and discharge status
options.feedback:
Right. The 2 is before the comma, so it picks a row. The blank after
the comma means *every column*. So you get one whole patient: 54,
O-, 118, not yet discharged.

A blank means "all of them", on whichever side it sits.

options.text: The `blood_type` column, since it's the second column
options.feedback:
That's what `patients[, 2]` would give — with the 2 *after* the
comma. Here it's before the comma, so it's picking a row.

options.text: Just `54`, the first value in row 2
options.feedback:
The blank after the comma means every column, not the first one. You
get the whole row.

options.text: An error — something is missing after the comma
options.feedback:
Leaving a side blank is allowed, and deliberate. It means "all of
them".

title: Two ways to get a column
prompt: Which of these gives you the same thing as `patients$age`?
hint: To get a column, the name has to be on the column side of the comma.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.feedback:
Right. Blank before the comma means every row; `"age"` after it picks
the column. You get the same vector as `patients$age`. You'll see
both in generated code, so it's worth recognising them as the same
thing.

This is the dangerous one. It puts `"age"` on the *row* side, and
asks for a row called "age". There isn't one — so instead of an
error, R gives you back a single row full of `NA`s. A misplaced comma
that fails silently.

Without quotes, R looks for a variable called `age`, and there isn't
one — `age` only exists as a column inside `patients`. Same lesson as
`labs$crp` in the last module.

That's the first *row* — one patient. The age column is every
patient's age.

title: More than one row
prompt: Get rows 1 and 5 — every column for both patients.
hint:
You need two numbers on the row side. You already know the function that
combines values.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
`c(1, 5)` makes a vector of two positions, and the brackets keep both
rows. Anything you can make a vector of, you can put on either side of
the comma.

checks.on_fail:
Not rows 1 and 5 yet. Put both positions together with `c()`, before
the comma.

match.pattern: undefined columns|unused argument|incorrect number of dimensions

misconceptions.feedback:
Writing `1, 5` on its own makes R read the 5 as the *column*. To give
the row side two numbers, combine them first: `c(1, 5)`.

title: Just the columns you need
prompt: Keep every patient, but only the `age` and `sbp` columns.
hint: Column names go after the comma, in quotes. You need two of them.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
Blank before the comma for every row, and a vector of two names after
it. Same idea as the last exercise, on the other side of the comma.

checks.on_fail:
That didn't give you exactly the `age` and `sbp` columns, in that
order.

misconceptions.feedback:
Column names need quotes inside square brackets. Without them, R
goes looking for variables called `age` and `sbp`, which don't
exist on their own.

title: Only the patients who went home
prompt:
The row side of the brackets can take TRUEs and FALSEs too, just as a
vector's could. Keep only the patients who have been discharged.
hint:
`patients$discharged` is already TRUE for exactly the rows you want. Which
side of the comma does it go on?
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
The TRUEs and FALSEs pick rows, and the blank after the comma keeps
every column. In module 7 you used one column to filter another; now
the same idea keeps whole patients.

checks.on_fail:
Not the three discharged patients yet. The TRUEs and FALSEs go before
the comma.

misconceptions.feedback:
R used your TRUEs and FALSEs to pick *columns* — five answers for
four columns — because they weren't before a comma. To choose
patients, the question goes on the row side: before the comma, with
the column side left blank.

Check the brackets. There's a `$` inside square brackets here, and
it's easy to lose track of which one you've closed.

title: Asking a question of the rows
prompt: Keep only the patients older than 60.
hint:
You need a question that's TRUE for each patient over 60. Ask it of the
`age` column.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
`patients$age > 60` asks each patient *are you over 60?* and gives
`TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE`. The brackets keep the rows that said
yes. This is how filtering works underneath, whatever it's written
as.

checks.on_fail: Not the three patients over 60 yet.

misconceptions.feedback:
No rows came back — and no error. That usually means a column name
is slightly wrong: `patients$Age` doesn't exist, so `$` quietly gives
back nothing, and a question asked of nothing keeps nothing. Check
the spelling and capitals against the table.

R used your TRUEs and FALSEs to pick *columns* — five answers for
four columns — because they weren't before a comma. To choose
patients, the question goes on the row side: before the comma, with
the column side left blank.

`age` only exists as a column inside `patients`. Write
`patients$age` so R knows where to find it.

title: A patient who doesn't exist
prompt:
You were handed this to find the patients with a systolic over 140.

```r
patients[patients$sbp > 140, ]
```

Remember that the 71-year-old's blood pressure is missing. How many rows
come back?
hint:
`patients$sbp > 140` gives `TRUE FALSE NA FALSE TRUE`. You saw what square
brackets do with an `NA` in module 6.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: 3 — the two high readings, plus a row that's entirely `NA`
options.feedback:
Right, and this is the one to remember from this module. The `NA` in
the question can't be kept or dropped, so R hands back a row of `NA`s
— no age, no blood type, nothing. It isn't the 71-year-old. It's a
patient who doesn't exist.

Count the rows and you'd report three patients over 140. There were
two.

That's the right answer to the question, but not what these brackets
give you. The missing reading produces an extra row of `NA`s, just as
it produced an extra `NA` in module 6.

options.text: 3 — including the 71-year-old, with a blank blood pressure
options.feedback:
Close, but worse than that. The extra row isn't the 71-year-old — it's
a row where *everything* is `NA`, including the age and blood type.
The patient has been replaced by nothing at all.

options.text: An error about the missing value
options.feedback:
No error. It returns something that looks exactly like a result, which
is what makes it dangerous.

title: Two questions at once
prompt:
To keep the phantom out, you need rows where the reading *isn't missing*
**and** is over 140. `&` means *and*: it gives TRUE only where both sides
are TRUE.

Check the question before you use it. What does this give?

```r
!is.na(patients$sbp) & patients$sbp > 140
```
hint:
Left side: `TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE`. Right side: `TRUE FALSE NA FALSE
TRUE`. Work through them in pairs — and think about what `FALSE and
unknown` must be.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.feedback:
Right — and look at the third one. The left side says FALSE, *not
missing* is false. The right side is `NA`. And `FALSE & NA` is
`FALSE`: if one half is definitely false, the whole thing is false,
whatever the unknown turns out to be. That's exactly why this works.
No `NA` left, so no phantom row.

That's the right side on its own. `&` combines both sides, and
`FALSE & NA` comes out FALSE — if one half is certainly false, the
answer is false no matter what the unknown is.

That's the left side on its own — which readings aren't missing. `&`
needs both sides to be TRUE.

title: Filter without the phantom
prompt:
Now use it. Keep only the patients whose systolic is recorded and over
140.
hint: The blank is the question you just checked.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
You've pulled two real patients, with no phantom. The line of code is
now longer than the first version, and every part of it is there for
a reason.

checks.on_fail: Not the two patients at 142 and 156 yet.

misconceptions.feedback:
R used your TRUEs and FALSEs to pick *columns* — five answers for
four columns — because they weren't before a comma. To choose
patients, the question goes on the row side: before the comma, with
the column side left blank.

That gives the right rows for these five patients, and no others. Add
a sixth patient and it would quietly keep the wrong ones. Write the
question, not its answer.

Comparing with `NA` never works — `== NA` and `!= NA` both give `NA`
for every row. To ask whether something is missing, use `is.na()`.

Three rows, so the phantom is still there. The question needs both
halves, joined with `&`.

title: Who is still in hospital?
prompt:
Store the patients who have *not* been discharged in `inpatients`, then
count them. `nrow()` counts the rows in a data frame.
hint: `!` turns TRUE into FALSE and FALSE into TRUE.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
`!patients$discharged` asks *who has not gone home?* The result is a
new, smaller data frame stored under its own name — and `patients`
itself is untouched. Filtering hands you a result; it never changes
the original unless you store over it.

checks.on_fail: `inpatients` should hold the two patients who haven't gone home.
The last line should count the rows in `inpatients`.

misconceptions.feedback:
Three — that's the patients who *have* gone home. Put `!` in front to
turn the question around.

title: The average of the older patients
prompt:
One more — nothing new, just things you already know turning up together.
Read this call from the inside out. What does it return?

```r
mean(patients[patients$age > 60, "sbp"])
```
hint:
First: which patients does the filter keep? Then: what are their blood
pressures?
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.feedback:
Right. Inside out: `patients$age > 60` keeps the patients aged 67, 71
and 62, and `"sbp"` after the comma takes their blood pressures —
`142 NA 156`. The 71-year-old's is missing, so `mean()` gives `NA`.

Nothing about the age filter was wrong — it kept exactly the right
patients. But a missing value came along with one of them, and when
you ask for an average that's missing a value, R says that average is
unknown unless you say `na.rm = TRUE`.

That's what you'd get with `na.rm = TRUE`. Without it, the missing
reading from the 71-year-old makes the whole average `NA`.

options.text: About `136.75` — the average of every recorded reading
options.feedback:
That's every patient's average. The filter keeps only the three over
60, so the 48- and 54-year-olds' readings aren't included.

It runs cleanly. That's the quiet kind of failure — it looks like a
number until you read it.

title: Numbers on both sides
prompt:
A column doesn't have to be named — you can pick it by its position,
counting from the left, the same way rows are counted from the top.

```r
patients[3, 2]
```

Click the value this picks out.
hint: Row 3 first. Then the second column along.

response.other:
Row first, then column — both counted from 1. Go down to row 3, then
across to the second column.

options.feedback:
Right — `B+`. Row 3, column 2. Numbers and names both work on either
side of the comma: `patients[3, 2]` and `patients[3, "blood_type"]`
pick exactly the same value.

Names are usually the better choice in code you write, because they
still point at the right column if the columns are ever reordered. But
you'll see numbers constantly in generated code, so it's worth reading
both fluently.

That's row 2, column 3 — the numbers read the other way round. The
first number is always the row.
